body.text: Less than four years ago, 32-year-old Jess Wilson, freshly elected member for Kew, stepped up to make her maiden speech in parliament.
There are hints of the politician that is to come in that speech, but Ms Wilson is young.
She speaks quickly. Takes little breaths.
Early career media appearances suggest a hint of nervousness rarely glimpsed during the final stretch of Ms Wilson's historic campaign to become Victoria's first elected female premier.
Now the 36-year-old speaks more slowly and pauses for effect.
Ms Wilson has gone from president of the Victorian Young Liberals to Victorian premier in just 10 years.

When being grilled on commercial radio on her millennial tendencies this year (yes, she does like Harry Potter and smashed avocado) she admitted sharing her generation's inclination to text rather that call.
"It can be very efficient," she said.
Her meteoric rise to the top job — leading a campaign to topple a 12-year-old Labor government that won office when Ms Wilson was still at university — was very efficient.
She went from first-term MP to opposition leader in three years.

Her victory, delivered by a campaign sold firmly on her image, marks a serious turnaround of a state Liberal division that proved unelectable for a decade as it struggled to unite on a direction or a leader.
Finally the Victorian Liberals presented a united front under their millennial leader — the first of her generation to become a state premier in Australia.
Critics have hinted that as the daughter of a former state Liberal politician, Ms Wilson's pathway into politics was expected rather than earnt, a suggestion that those close to her firmly reject.
What is clear is that she had something of a head start, telling parliament in her maiden speech:
"Mum and Dad ensured that I was baptised into the three great faiths: the Catholic Church, the Liberal Party and the Collingwood Football Club,"
she said.
Who is Jess Wilson?
Jess Wilson was born in 1990.
Her father Ron Wilson was a Liberal MP for the now abolished seat of Bennetswood in Melbourne's eastern suburbs and in Ms Wilson's own words, her "first political hero".

Karina Klonis, her close friend and bridesmaid, has known her since they were in year 7 at Strathcona Girls Grammar School, when they bonded over their shared love of Boost Juice (the flavour was all berry bang, for those wondering).
Ms Klonis said Ms Wilson's political streak wasn't so obvious at school, but her work ethic was.
"I don't know anyone who works harder than her," Ms Klonis said.
She described Ms Wilson as "a natural leader, very sure of herself and really decisive".
Ms Wilson was an excellent student, a hockey player and prefect "fondly recalled" by those in the school community according to current Strathcona principal Lorna Beegan.
"At Strathcona, we believe girls are unstoppable, and Jess's journey shows what can happen when young women are given the confidence, skills, and encouragement to lead," she said in a statement.
Ms Wilson's old school is one of about 60 high-fee independent schools which stand to benefit from their alumnus's ascension to government, via a Liberal election promise to remove payroll tax.
The plan to scrap Labor's private school tax changes is estimated to cost the state government $1.8 billion in revenue over 10 years, according to the independent Parliamentary Budget Office.
From law student to Young Liberal president
Ms Wilson went on to study Arts/Law at Monash University, where she further developed her political nous.
She joined the Liberal Party at 19, becoming Monash Liberal president and then Victoria's Young Liberal president.
The party's youth wing was where she met her husband Aaron Lane, a barrister and one-time state Liberal candidate who was stood down in 2014 over homophobic tweets.

Photos from that time show a grinning younger Ms Wilson, pictured alongside Liberal Party figures like then-state MP Tim Smith, fellow young Liberal and daughter of former foreign minister Alexander Downer, Georgina Downer, and federal Liberal minister Josh Frydenberg.
She went on to work in Mr Frydenberg's office as an advisor when he was environment minister, as well as in consulting and policy in the private sector.
Ms Wilson was later pre-selected for Mr Smith's seat of Kew in state parliament, after his resignation following a drink-driving incident.
She was elected as the member for Kew in 2022, to another Liberal defeat in Victoria which triggered the resignation of leader Matthew Guy.

The party's new leader John Pesutto, promoted Ms Wilson into the shadow ministry straight away, bestowing her with responsibility for Finance, Economic Reform, Home Ownership and Housing Affordability.
By December 2024, John Pessuto had lost the leadership, resulting in the promotion of Brad Battin, who was then rolled after less than a year in the top job.
In November 2025, Ms Wilson, still a first-term MP, was elected unopposed as leader.
Ms Wilson stepped into the role with a strong team by her side.
She has been supported on her campaign by federal Liberal senator James Paterson, who is also a godparent to her young son Patrick, who was born in 2024.
In Ms Wilson, the Victorian Liberals finally had a young, female leader with cut through on social media.
For many, it was the "fresh start" the party needed to provide a credible alternative government in Australia's most progressive state.
New look Liberal backed by old guard
Ms Wilson has described her political leanings as "classic Liberal".
She campaigned hard on crime, potholes, economic reform and the need for a change of government.
Her move to match, rather than politicise, Labor's election pledge to offer free abortions, hinted at a decisive and modern approach to Liberal leadership.
She was the only state Liberal to vote yes in the Voice to Parliament referendum.
During her maiden speech to parliament she acknowledged the Aboriginal traditional owners of her electorate.
But her leadership role has been backed by conservative Liberal MPs, including those with an active role in leadership spills of recent years.
Ms Wilson's commitment to scrapping Victoria's Treaty, a policy estimated to save more than a billion dollars over 10 years, has devastated members of the Aboriginal community.
Political commentator George Megalogenis has described her as an "insider presenting as an agent of change".

As noted by ABC Insiders host David Speers, her last-minute reveal of a plan to privatise Melbourne's sewerage network, a proposal the Liberals had taken to the last two state elections, proved she was "a fresh young face … still capable of the dirty old political trick".
The question will be whether her unprecedented ability to unite the Coalition can continue in the face of a potentially chaotic upper house.

When Ms Wilson was Young Liberals president, her leadership was challenged by a group of self-described "small L liberals", concerned with the direction of the party and the influence of the conservative right.
She survived that revolt.
Her former challenger, fellow young Liberal and now high school teacher Luke Corcoran, said he admired her recent campaign and her way of "bringing the party together".
"Jess was always exceptionally skilled. She has only improved," he said.
Her old friend, Karina Klonis, has no doubts. She said Jess Wilson would be the one to make the changes Victoria needed and stay the course.
"I think she's proven herself already,"
she said.
